items.followUp: Name the three stages of the cell cycle’s interphase.

rubric.why: All three stages of interphase are required.
rubric.description: Names the three phases of interphase.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for all three phases; award 1 mark if two phases are correct.

modelAnswer: The three phases of interphase are G₁ phase, S phase and G₂ phase.

items.followUp: State one difference between mitosis and meiosis.

rubric.why: Identifies the different kinds of cells in which these divisions typically occur.
rubric.description: Correctly contrasts the cells or organisms in which mitosis and binary fission occur.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that mitosis occurs in eukaryotic cells and binary fission typically occurs in prokaryotes.

rubric.why: States a distinguishing feature of the division process or its outcome.
rubric.description: Gives a correct difference in the process or outcome.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that mitosis involves nuclear division followed by cell division, while binary fission divides one cell into two.

modelAnswer: Mitosis is cell division in eukaryotic cells; it involves division of the nucleus before the cell divides.
Binary fission is a simpler division in which a prokaryotic cell divides into two daughter cells.

rubric.why: Shows that somatic cells are the non-reproductive cells of the body.
rubric.description: Identifies somatic cells as body cells, rather than reproductive cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing them as body or non-reproductive cells.

rubric.why: Adds a common defining feature of somatic cells.
rubric.description: States that somatic cells generally contain two sets of chromosomes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as diploid.

modelAnswer: Somatic cells are the body cells other than the reproductive cells (gametes).
They are generally diploid, containing two sets of chromosomes.

items.followUp: Name the three types of subunits that make up an ATP molecule.

rubric.why: Identifies the nitrogenous base and sugar components of ATP.
Identifies the phosphate component of ATP.
rubric.description: Names the phosphate groups, including that there are three.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the phosphate groups.

modelAnswer: ATP is made of adenine, ribose sugar and three phosphate groups.
Two of its components are adenine and ribose sugar.

items.followUp: Draw a labelled graph showing how enzyme activity changes as substrate concentration increases.

rubric.why: The graph must identify the variables on both axes.
rubric.description: Labels the temperature and enzyme activity axes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly labelling the horizontal axis as temperature and the vertical axis as rate of enzyme action or activity.

rubric.why: Shows that enzyme activity rises to an optimum and then falls at higher temperatures.
rubric.description: Shows the characteristic rise to an optimum followed by a steep decline.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correctly shaped curve, with activity increasing to an optimum and then decreasing at high temperature.

modelAnswer: Draw the horizontal axis as temperature (°C), from 0 to 60, using 10°C per division.
Draw the vertical axis as relative rate of enzyme action (%), from 0 to 100, using 10% per division.
Plot the representative points (temperature, relative rate): (0°C, 0%), (20°C, 50%), (37°C, 100%) and (60°C, 0%).
Join the points with a smooth curve that rises to a peak near 37°C and then falls sharply. Label the peak as the optimum temperature.

items.followUp: What happens to the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction when substrate concentration is increased after all active sites are occupied?

rubric.why: Defines saturation in terms of substrate occupying the enzyme active sites.
rubric.description: States that all enzyme active sites are occupied by substrate.

rubric.why: Explains the consequence of active-site saturation for reaction rate.
rubric.description: States that the reaction is at its maximum rate and further substrate does not increase it.

modelAnswer: Active sites are saturated when substrate molecules occupy all the available active sites of the enzymes.
The reaction is then at its maximum rate, so adding more substrate does not increase the rate.

items.followUp: Which two food components provide about 4 kilocalories of energy per gram each?

rubric.why: Carbohydrates provide approximately 4 kilocalories of energy per gram.
Proteins provide approximately 4 kilocalories of energy per gram.

modelAnswer: Carbohydrates and proteins provide the same amount of energy per gram.
Each provides about 4 kilocalories (approximately 17 kilojoules) per gram.

items.followUp: Explain how transpiration helps in the upward movement of water and minerals in a plant.

rubric.why: Identifies water loss from leaves as the cause of the pulling force.
rubric.description: Explains that evaporation of water from leaves produces a pulling force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking transpiration from leaves with the pull.

rubric.why: States the importance of the pull in transporting water and dissolved minerals upward.
rubric.description: Explains that the pull helps move water, and dissolved minerals, from roots toward the leaves through the xylem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for its role in the upward transport of water or minerals.

modelAnswer: Transpirational pull is the pulling force created in the xylem when water evaporates from the leaves during transpiration.
It helps draw water and dissolved minerals from the roots up through the xylem to the leaves; this upward movement is called the ascent of sap.
